newsitem.title: USA: Intel worries shake entire market.
newsitem.headline: Intel worries shake entire market.

text.p: With a sudden and stunning display of vulnerability, Intel Corp showed in a flash what happens to a stock market when its leaders stumble.

Intel, a source of support for the market during weak times and leadership during rallies, unleashed a torrent of selling with its warning early Friday that its second quarter results would fail to meet expectations.

"This is a bellwether event," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "Intel is such a force that to the extent that you use benchmarks, it is one of the benchmarks that you use."
Within minutes of the U.S. stock market open, Intel shares plummeted 18 points to 145-3/4. The Dow industrials slid 70 points to 7260, triggering program trading curbs just moments after the opening.
The sell-off hammered the entire technology sector, dragging the Nasdaq Composite down 40 points to 1363.
"We're back where we were 10 days ago," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "Ten too-good days ago."
What made this morning's announcement by Intel particularly startling was the simple fact that unlike fellow technology bellwether Microsoft Corp, Intel has rarely cautioned investors.
"It seems like Microsoft every quarter is warning about slowdowns in its business," Bleier said. "Intel, on the other hand, seldom does."
Analysts said certain aspects of Intel's warning, particularly comments about weak demand in Europe, were especially troubling.

"If they're having problems with demand, that raises questions about demand for boxes," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management."And given the interconnectivity of technology, the news has set off a domino effect that has forced the whole sector to implode."
Analysts also noted the market, fresh off a sizzling six-week surge that added nearly 1,000 Dow points and 200 points to the Nasdaq Composite, was vulnerable to bad news.
"It's been our perspective that the Dow was fully valued and the market was looking for a catalyst to take it lower," Orlando said. "I would argue this may be the catalyst."
